::: callout-note
## Scope

This vignette derives the intervals and tests for the single-cell
mixture fitted by
[`deconvolute_single_cell()`](../reference/deconvolute_single_cell.html):
one bulk sample, one single-cell reference, a composition on the
simplex and two technical scales estimated with it. The model, the
closed-form scales and the profile Newton fit are in the
[single-cell generative and optimisation vignette](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-profile-newton).
The population-level counterpart, with the regularity conditions, the
three first-order tests and the boundary theory that this vignette
reuses, is the
[population inference vignette](01-2-population-inference.html).

1. @sec-sc-setting states the model and its scale equivariance.
2. @sec-sc-information gives the information matrix and the Schur
   complement that carries the cost of estimating the scales.
3. @sec-sc-small-dispersion states the limit that justifies a
   first-order interval for one bulk sample.
4. @sec-sc-intervals derives the six interval methods of
   [`confint_single_cell()`](../reference/confint_single_cell.html), and
   @sec-sc-reml the calibration for few genes.
5. @sec-sc-nuisance gives the intervals for the scales,
   @sec-sc-tests the likelihood-ratio tests and the boundary, and
   @sec-sc-limits what none of these intervals covers.
:::

{{< include _notation.qmd >}}

# Model and scale equivariance {#sec-sc-setting}

For bulk sample $i$ with $n_i$ cells and capture ratio $a_i$, the
averaged mixture of independent cells is

$$
\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{p}
\sim\mathcal{N}_G\bigl(c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p},\;\phi\,\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_{j=1}^{J}p_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j},
\qquad
c=a_in_i,\quad\phi=a_i^{2}n_i,
$$ {#eq-sc-model}

with $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$ the mean of a type-$j$ cell on raw
counts and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ its within-type covariance. The
composition is charted by
$\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho})$
with a Helmert basis $\mathbf{V}$
([ILR chart](01-1-population-generative-optimisation.html#sec-ilr)).
Concentrating the scales out gives the profile log-likelihood

$$
\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})
=-\frac{G}{2}\log Q(\boldsymbol{p})
-\frac12\log\det\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})+\text{const},
\qquad
Q(\boldsymbol{p})=\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{r}},
$$ {#eq-sc-profile-recap}

with $\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}=\boldsymbol{y}-\hat c(\boldsymbol{p})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}$ the
generalised least-squares residual
([closed-form scales](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-profile-scales)).

**Scale equivariance.** Multiply the bulk by $k>0$. The closed forms
give $\hat c(k\boldsymbol{y})=k\hat c(\boldsymbol{y})$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}$ scales by $k$,
$Q$ by $k^{2}$ and $\hat\phi$ by $k^{2}$, so

$$
\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho};k\boldsymbol{y})=\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho};\boldsymbol{y})-G\log k .
$$ {#eq-sc-equivariance}

The shift does not depend on $\boldsymbol{\rho}$. The estimate $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$,
the profile Hessian, every interval built from them and every
likelihood ratio are unchanged, while $(\hat c,\hat\phi)$ move to
$(k\hat c,k^{2}\hat\phi)$. The capture ratio and the number of cells enter
only through $c$ and $\phi$. A fixed capture ratio is therefore a
relabelling of the scales and cannot change the composition, which is
why a simulation study need not cross it with the other factors.

# Information and the Schur complement {#sec-sc-information}

Write $\boldsymbol{\eta}=(c,\phi)$, $\boldsymbol{W}=\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}$ and
$\boldsymbol{m}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}$. The expected information of
@eq-sc-model has the blocks

$$
I_{c\phi}=0,\qquad
I_{\phi\phi}=\frac{G}{2\phi^{2}},\qquad
I_{cc}=\frac{\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{m}}{\phi},\qquad
I_{p_jc}=\frac{c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{m}}{\phi},\qquad
I_{p_j\phi}=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j})}{2\phi}.
$$ {#eq-sc-information}

The two scales are orthogonal to each other, but neither is orthogonal
to the composition. The asymptotic covariance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ is
therefore the inverse of the Schur complement

$$
I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}\mid\boldsymbol{\eta}}
=I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}\boldsymbol{\rho}}
-I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}\boldsymbol{\eta}}I_{\boldsymbol{\eta}\boldsymbol{\eta}}^{-1}I_{\boldsymbol{\eta}\boldsymbol{\rho}},
$$ {#eq-sc-schur}

which is never larger than $I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}\boldsymbol{\rho}}$: estimating the
scales widens the composition intervals, and the Schur complement
accounts for it without a separate correction. When an interest
parameter is orthogonal to the nuisance, its standard error is the same
whether the nuisance is known or estimated
[@coxParameterOrthogonalityApproximate1987]; @eq-sc-information shows
that this does not happen here. A scalar interest parameter can always
be made orthogonal by reparametrisation; a vector one in general
cannot.

The fit uses the observed counterpart. By the envelope theorem the
negative Hessian of the profile log-likelihood @eq-sc-profile-recap is
the Schur complement of the observed information at the closed-form
scales
([profile Hessian](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-profile-derivatives)),
so profile-based and joint Wald intervals coincide.
[`vcov_single_cell()`](../reference/vcov_single_cell.html) and the fit
return

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})=\bigl(-\nabla^{2}\ell^{\ast}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})\bigr)^{-1},
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})
=\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}\,\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})\,\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\top},
$$ {#eq-sc-vcov}

as `vcov_rho` and `vcov`, with $\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}$ the
[ILR Jacobian](01-1-population-generative-optimisation.html#sec-ilr-deriv).
The complementary Schur complement, which removes $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ from
the scale block, gives `vcov_nuisance` for $(c,\phi)$.

# Small-dispersion asymptotics in the number of cells {#sec-sc-small-dispersion}

One bulk sample has no replicate, so the usual limit in the number of
independent observations does not apply, and the $G$ genes are not
independent replicates either. Divide the bulk by $c$: the per-cell bulk
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}=\boldsymbol{y}/c$ satisfies

$$
\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}_G\bigl(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p},\;n^{-1}\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr),
\qquad n=c^{2}/\phi,
$$ {#eq-sc-per-cell}

a family whose dispersion $1/n$ shrinks as the number of cells grows.
That is the small-dispersion limit of
@jørgensenSmallDispersionAsymptotics1987. Under it the maximum-likelihood
estimate is asymptotically normal around the realised composition,
with covariance the inverse of @eq-sc-schur, and the likelihood-ratio
statistic is asymptotically $\chi^{2}$. The approximation improves with
the number of cells of every type, $m_j=np_j$, not with $G$. The number
of genes enters through the residual degrees of freedom of the
covariance scale (@sec-sc-reml). With Gaussian cells the sum is exactly
Gaussian at any $n$; with counts, @eq-sc-per-cell is a central-limit
approximation that needs every $m_j$ to be large.

# Intervals for the composition {#sec-sc-intervals}

[`confint_single_cell()`](../reference/confint_single_cell.html) takes the
bulk and the reference moments, refits, and returns one of six
intervals. Its `estimate` is the composition that the likelihood
optimises, before any conversion between cell and transcript fractions.

| `method` | Interval | Inside $[0,1]$ | On a face |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `"wald"` | $\hat p_j\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{SE}_j$ from @eq-sc-vcov | no | undefined |
| `"ilr"` (default) | Wald in $\boldsymbol{\rho}$, mapped by $\boldsymbol{\psi}$ | yes | undefined |
| `"profile"` | likelihood-ratio inversion, scales concentrated out | yes | needs the boundary test |
| `"firth"` | Wald at the penalised estimate, also mapped by $\boldsymbol{\psi}$ | ILR version only | estimate stays interior |
| `"bootstrap"` | parametric percentile | yes | automatic |
| `"reference"` | percentile over resampled references | yes | automatic |

: Composition intervals of the single-cell mixture. {#tbl-sc-intervals}

**Delta method.** The `"wald"` interval uses the diagonal of
@eq-sc-vcov [@oehlertNoteDeltaMethod1992]. It is symmetric and can leave
$[0,1]$ for a rare type.

**Inverse ILR chart.** The `"ilr"` interval forms the Wald interval in
$\boldsymbol{\rho}$ and maps it back. For $J=2$ the endpoints of the single
coordinate are mapped by $\boldsymbol{\psi}$. For $J>2$, draws
$\boldsymbol{\rho}^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}},\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})\bigr)$,
$b=1,\ldots,$`n_draws`, are mapped to $\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho}^{(b)})$
and the interval is the marginal quantile of each proportion. Every
draw is a composition, so the interval stays inside the simplex. Pass
`seed` for a reproducible Monte Carlo map.

**Profile likelihood.** The `"profile"` interval
([`confint_profile_single_cell()`](../reference/confint_profile_single_cell.html))
fixes $p_j$ at a trial value, refits the other proportions and both
scales with
[`restricted_mle_single_cell()`](../reference/restricted_mle_single_cell.html),
and keeps the values whose deviance stays below the
$\chi^{2}_{1}$ quantile [@wilksLargeSampleDistributionLikelihood1938].
It does not depend on the chart and stays in $[0,1]$. An endpoint that
lands on a face is not a Wilks interval and must be read with the
boundary test of @sec-sc-tests.

**Firth penalty.** The `"firth"` interval maximises
$\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})+\tfrac12\log\det\{-\nabla^{2}\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})\}$
([`fit_firth_single_cell()`](../reference/fit_firth_single_cell.html))
[@firthBiasReductionMaximum1993], then reports the Wald interval at the
penalised estimate. The penalty uses the observed profile information,
with the scales concentrated out, so it adds no free scale. The
information in $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ inherits the factor $\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})$ of the
ILR Jacobian, whose determinant vanishes at a face, so the penalty
tends to $-\infty$ there and the penalised estimate is always interior.
Firth's exact removal of the first-order bias holds for the canonical
parameter of an exponential family; this curved Gaussian family needs a
simulation check
([Firth penalisation](01-2-population-inference.html#sec-firth)).

**Parametric bootstrap.** The `"bootstrap"` interval
([`bootstrap_single_cell()`](../reference/bootstrap_single_cell.html))
draws
$\boldsymbol{Y}^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\hat c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\hat{\boldsymbol{p}},\hat\phi\,\boldsymbol{S}_W(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})\bigr)$,
refits the profile model, and returns percentile intervals for the
composition and for both scales [@efronBootstrapMethodsAnother1979]. The
reference moments stay fixed.

**Reference bootstrap.** The `"reference"` interval
([`reference_bootstrap_single_cell()`](../reference/reference_bootstrap_single_cell.html))
propagates the uncertainty of the reference itself. When every type
has at least two donors it resamples donors within each type, rebuilds
$(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j})$ and refits the observed bulk.
With one donor it resamples cells within each type and regenerates the
bulk from the fitted model with the original moments, then refits with
the resampled moments. Drawing that bulk from the resampled moments
instead would hide the reference error, since the bulk and the
reference would then agree by construction. Shuffling cell-type labels
is not an interval: the fitted composition moves with the labels, which
is equivariance, not sampling variability.

## Few genes: the REML calibration {#sec-sc-reml}

The covariance scale is estimated from the whitened residual,
$\hat\phi=Q(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})/G$, after fitting $J$ mean parameters
($J-1$ coordinates of $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ and $c$). It has
$\nu=G-J$ residual degrees of freedom, and the maximum-likelihood
divisor $G$ biases it downwards by a factor of about $\nu/G$. Every
interval that plugs in $\hat\phi$ is then too narrow when $G$ is small:
with $G=20$ and $J=4$, $\nu/G=0.8$.

`variance = "reml"` in `confint_single_cell()` and
`confint_profile_single_cell()` corrects for those degrees of freedom,
as restricted maximum likelihood does for a variance component:

- the covariances of @eq-sc-vcov are inflated by $G/\nu$;
- Wald and ILR quantiles come from $t_{\nu}$ instead of the normal, with
  a multivariate $t$ for the Monte Carlo ILR map when $J>2$;
- $\phi$ gets the chi-square interval
  $\bigl[G\hat\phi/\chi^{2}_{\nu;1-\alpha/2},\;G\hat\phi/\chi^{2}_{\nu;\alpha/2}\bigr]$;
- the profile interval uses the cut-off

$$
D_{\alpha}=G\log\Bigl(1+\frac{F_{1,\nu;1-\alpha}}{\nu}\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-sc-reml-cutoff}

  in place of $\chi^{2}_{1;1-\alpha}$.

@eq-sc-reml-cutoff is exact in a linear model with an unknown variance:
with the variance profiled out, twice the log likelihood ratio for one
linear constraint equals $G\log(1+F/\nu)$ for an $F_{1,\nu}$ statistic.
As $\nu\to\infty$ it tends to $\chi^{2}_{1}$. The bootstrap methods
ignore `variance`, because they draw $\hat\phi$ afresh in every
replicate. The Monte Carlo check of these calibrations is
`scripts/benchmark_metrics/check_confidence_interval_coverage.R`:
the maximum-likelihood intervals under-cover with $G=10$ genes, and the
REML calibration brings them back to the nominal level.

# Intervals for the two scales {#sec-sc-nuisance}

`confint_single_cell()` also returns `nuisance`, intervals for $c$ and
$\phi$. The default `nuisance$interval` is a Wald interval on
$(\log c,\log\phi)$ from the complementary Schur complement, which
removes $\boldsymbol{\rho}$, mapped back by the exponential, so both limits
are positive. `nuisance$interval_wald` is the symmetric normal interval
on $(c,\phi)$ itself. Under `variance = "reml"`, $\phi$ gets the
chi-square interval of @sec-sc-reml. The bootstrap methods replace both
with percentile intervals.

$I_{c\phi}=0$ does not reduce this block to two one-parameter problems:
the complement still accounts for the estimation of the composition.
The derived quantities $\hat a=\hat\phi/\hat c$ and $\hat n=\hat c^{2}/\hat\phi$
inherit the downward bias of $\hat\phi$, so $\hat n$ is biased upwards.
They describe the sample; $\hat n$ is a number of cells only when the
capture ratio is known, from the same platform or from paired samples
[@erdmann-phamLikelihoodbasedDeconvolutionBulk2021].

# Likelihood-ratio tests and the boundary {#sec-sc-tests}

[`lrt_single_cell()`](../reference/lrt_single_cell.html) tests a value
of the composition with the scales profiled out under both hypotheses.
An interior null, $p_j=c_0\in(0,1)$, is calibrated by $\chi^{2}$ with as
many degrees of freedom as constraints. A null on a face,
$p_j=0$, puts the true parameter on the boundary of the simplex: the
limit is the projection of a Gaussian score on the tangent cone, and
for one absent type with orthogonal information the statistic follows
$\tfrac12\chi^{2}_{0}+\tfrac12\chi^{2}_{1}$
[@hermanDistributionLikelihoodRatio1954; @selfAsymptoticPropertiesMaximum1987].
`lrt_single_cell()` counts the null proportions on the boundary and
switches to the chi-bar-square calibration automatically. The restricted
fit on a face,
[`restricted_mle_single_cell()`](../reference/restricted_mle_single_cell.html),
uses the same trust-region Newton driver on the remaining coordinates,
with the scales concentrated out. The theory and the chi-bar-square
weights are in the
[population inference vignette](01-2-population-inference.html#sec-boundary).

The L-BFGS-B branch of `deconvolute_single_cell()` can return an exact
zero. There the ILR coordinates, the Wald covariances and the Wald and
ILR intervals are undefined (`NA`); the profile interval and the
boundary test are the procedures that remain valid.

# What these intervals do not cover {#sec-sc-limits}

- **The reference is a plug-in.** Every method except the reference
  bootstrap treats $(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j})$ as known. No
  sandwich or higher-order term corrects for the estimation of
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$; the reference bootstrap is the implemented
  route.
- **One donor has no between-donor layer.** $\phi$ inflates the
  covariance globally but cannot correct its shape, so with a reference
  from one donor the intervals describe within-donor variation only.
- **The variance function must be right.** The determinant term of the
  likelihood adds information only if $\phi\,\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})$ is the
  true covariance. Otherwise the quasi-score of the
  [generalised linear model view](01-2-population-inference.html#sec-glm)
  is the safer estimator.
- **Gaussian cells.** The sum of Gaussian cells is exactly Gaussian. For
  count data, @eq-sc-per-cell is a central-limit approximation that needs
  many cells of every type.

| Question | Procedure | Function |
|:--|:--|:--|
| interval for a proportion, interior estimate | ILR inverse chart, or profile | `confint_single_cell(method = "ilr")`, `confint_profile_single_cell()` |
| few genes, $G-J$ small | the same, with the REML calibration | `variance = "reml"` |
| proportion close to zero | Firth penalty, or profile | `confint_single_cell(method = "firth")` |
| is type $j$ absent? | boundary likelihood-ratio test | `lrt_single_cell()` |
| no trust in the asymptotics | parametric bootstrap | `bootstrap_single_cell()` |
| uncertainty of the reference | reference bootstrap | `reference_bootstrap_single_cell()` |
| capture ratio and number of cells | log-scale Wald or REML chi-square | `confint_single_cell()$nuisance` |
